interventions.title: Legume-based cover cropping in the fallow window
interventions.what_to_do: Sow a legume cover mix (sunn hemp, cowpea, horse gram) into the fallow window instead of leaving soil bare; terminate by rolling or shallow incorporation two weeks before the main crop.
causal_chain: bare-soil days reduced -> surface temperature and evaporation fall
root exudates + biomass return -> soil organic carbon rises
organic carbon rises -> aggregate stability and water holding capacity rise
moist, carbon-rich topsoil -> microbial and mesofaunal diversity rise
flowering legumes -> pollinator forage in an otherwise empty window
interventions.why_it_works: Soil organic carbon is not just a fertility number; it is the habitat variable for the soil food web. Bare fallow in semi-arid systems oxidises carbon fastest because surface temperature peaks with no canopy. A legume cover crop removes the bare-soil window, fixes nitrogen so the carbon that accumulates has a usable C:N ratio, and adds a flowering resource for pollinators at a time of year when the landscape offers none.
interventions.trade_offs: Consumes residual soil moisture. In years with under ~300 mm rainfall the cover crop can compete with the following main crop unless terminated early.

interventions.title: Alley cropping with nitrogen-fixing tree hedgerows
interventions.what_to_do: Plant hedgerows of Leucaena, Gliricidia or Faidherbia at 8-12 m spacing across the slope, cropping the alleys; prune twice a year and return the prunings as mulch.
causal_chain: hedgerow canopy -> windspeed and evaporative demand at crop level fall
deep tree roots -> nutrients and water lifted from below the crop rooting zone
pruning mulch -> continuous carbon input to topsoil
permanent woody strips -> nesting and perching structure for birds and arthropods
linear habitat across the field -> reduced habitat fragmentation between remnant patches
interventions.why_it_works: In semi-arid croplands the binding constraint is usually water, not nutrients, and water losses are dominated by evaporation rather than transpiration. Hedgerows cut wind run and shade the soil surface, which changes the evaporation term directly. At the same time the woody strips are the only permanent vegetation in the system, so they carry the resident bird and predatory-arthropod community that annual crops cannot support, which in turn suppresses pest outbreaks.
interventions.trade_offs: Immediate loss of 10-15% cropped area and a 2-4 year establishment period before net benefit. Needs protection from grazing in year 1-2.

interventions.title: Replace monoculture with a cereal-legume intercrop
interventions.what_to_do: Move from sole wheat/rice to a 2:1 or 4:2 row intercrop with a pulse (chickpea, pigeon pea, lentil) matched to the rainfall window.
causal_chain: two root architectures -> soil profile explored at two depths
canopy closes earlier -> less bare soil evaporation and weed pressure
legume nitrogen fixation -> lower synthetic N -> less nitrate leaching
two flowering periods -> longer forage window for pollinators
structural and chemical diversity -> pest specialists diluted, natural enemies supported
interventions.why_it_works: Monoculture is a biodiversity problem and a risk problem at once. A single root architecture mines one soil layer, a single phenology gives one narrow forage window, and a single host makes specialist pests cheap to maintain. Intercropping changes all three at no land cost, and the land equivalent ratio in cereal-legume systems is typically above 1, so total productivity per hectare usually rises even when each component yields less.
interventions.trade_offs: Mechanised sowing and harvest get harder; row configuration has to match available equipment.

interventions.title: Residue retention with reduced tillage
interventions.what_to_do: Stop residue burning and removal; retain 30-50% of crop residue as surface mulch and shift to zero or minimum tillage seeding.
causal_chain: surface mulch -> soil surface temperature falls 3-6 C at peak
lower temperature + cover -> evaporation losses fall
no inversion tillage -> fungal hyphal networks and earthworm burrows survive
intact macropores -> infiltration rises, runoff and erosion fall
stable habitat -> soil macrofauna abundance and diversity rise
interventions.why_it_works: Tillage is the single most destructive routine event in a cropped soil's year: it shatters aggregates, exposes protected carbon to oxidation, and severs the mycorrhizal networks that take months to rebuild. Residue burning compounds it by removing the carbon input entirely. Retaining residue and stopping inversion tillage is therefore two interventions in one, and it is the cheapest carbon gain available on degraded cropland.

effects.magnitude: +0.1-0.4 t C/ha/yr in the 0-15 cm layer

interventions.trade_offs: Weed pressure rises in the first 2-3 seasons; needs a zero-till seed drill. On poorly drained clay soils surface residue can delay warming and sowing.

interventions.title: Farm pond plus contour bunding for in-situ water harvesting
interventions.what_to_do: Excavate a farm pond sized to 2-4% of the catchment area, fed by contour bunds or a graded field drain; leave one gently sloping bank unlined and vegetated.
causal_chain: runoff intercepted -> groundwater recharge and dry-season water availability rise
supplemental irrigation possible -> crop survives mid-season dry spells
standing water + vegetated bank -> amphibian breeding habitat and bird watering point created
aquatic vegetation -> odonate and aquatic invertebrate colonisation
reduced runoff velocity -> topsoil and nutrients retained on the field
interventions.why_it_works: In semi-arid systems the limiting factor for both crops and fauna is not annual rainfall but its distribution: the water arrives in a few intense events and leaves as runoff within hours. Storing a fraction of that runoff converts a pulse into a buffer. The biodiversity gain is disproportionate because standing water is the scarcest habitat type in a dry agricultural landscape, so a single pond can function as a stepping stone for amphibians and waterbirds across a whole cluster of farms.

effects.magnitude: new breeding habitat where none existed

interventions.trade_offs: Capital cost and 2-5% land take. A fully lined pond gains storage but loses recharge and most of the biodiversity value, so the design choice matters. Poorly sited ponds can intercept flows that downstream users depend on.

interventions.title: Native flowering hedgerow and uncropped field margin
interventions.what_to_do: Establish a 2-3 m strip of native flowering shrubs and grasses along field boundaries, staggering species so something is in flower in every month; cut on rotation, never all at once.
causal_chain: continuous floral resource -> pollinator populations persist through the year, not just at crop bloom
overwintering structure -> predatory beetles and spiders survive between seasons
resident natural enemies -> pest suppression at crop emergence when it matters most
linear connected strips -> movement corridor between remnant habitat patches
root mass at field edge -> nutrient interception before runoff leaves the field
interventions.why_it_works: Most pollinator loss on farmland is not caused by the absence of crop flowers but by the hungry gap either side of the crop bloom. A crop that flowers for three weeks cannot sustain a bee population for twelve months. The hedgerow's value is that it closes that gap, so the pollinators are already present and abundant when the crop needs them. The same strip doubles as the overwintering refuge for the predatory arthropods that control early-season pests.
interventions.trade_offs: Small land take and an annual maintenance cost. Benefits fall off sharply beyond ~50 m into large fields, so very large blocks need internal strips too.

interventions.title: Rotational grazing with enforced rest periods
interventions.what_to_do: Divide the grazing area into 4-8 paddocks, graze each for a short period, and rest each for long enough that palatable perennials complete regrowth before being grazed again.
causal_chain: rest period -> palatable perennial grasses rebuild root reserves
perennial root mass recovers -> soil carbon and infiltration rise
ground cover returns -> surface sealing and runoff fall
structural heterogeneity across paddocks -> grassland bird and insect niches restored
unpalatable invader species lose their competitive release
interventions.why_it_works: Continuous grazing is selective grazing: animals return to the same palatable plants every time they regrow, so those species exhaust their root reserves and die out while unpalatable species take over. The damage is caused by the frequency of defoliation, not the number of animals. Rotation fixes the frequency without necessarily reducing the herd, which is why it is adoptable where destocking is not.
interventions.trade_offs: Needs fencing or active herding and daily labour. Evidence on the carbon benefit is genuinely contested; the vegetation and hydrology benefits are better supported than the carbon claim.

interventions.title: Assisted natural regeneration on degraded land
interventions.what_to_do: Protect the site from fire and grazing, cut back competing grass around existing rootstock and saplings, and let the surviving root systems resprout instead of planting nursery seedlings.
causal_chain: existing rootstock released from competition -> rapid resprouting with an established root system
native species composition preserved -> local fauna find the plant species they co-evolved with
canopy closes -> microclimate cools, soil moisture is retained
litter layer builds -> soil carbon and decomposer diversity rise
structural complexity returns -> multi-layer habitat for birds, bats and arthropods
interventions.why_it_works: Degraded land is rarely biologically empty: it usually holds a large bank of suppressed rootstock and a viable seed bank. Those root systems are years ahead of any nursery seedling and cost nothing. Plantation with a few fast-growing exotics gives faster canopy but a much poorer species assemblage, which is why plantations can score well on tree cover and badly on biodiversity.

effects.magnitude: site dependent, typically visible by year 3-5

interventions.trade_offs: Requires sustained exclusion of grazing and fire, which is a social problem more than a technical one. Slower visible canopy than plantation, which makes it harder to fund.

interventions.title: Integrated pest management with economic threshold spraying
interventions.what_to_do: Scout weekly, spray only above an established economic threshold, rotate modes of action, and switch broad-spectrum products for selective ones during crop bloom.
causal_chain: fewer broad-spectrum applications -> predatory arthropod populations survive
predators survive -> secondary pest outbreaks and resurgence fall
lower spray load during bloom -> pollinator mortality falls
reduced runoff of actives -> aquatic invertebrate diversity in field drains recovers
mode-of-action rotation -> resistance development slowed, longevity of the tool preserved
interventions.why_it_works: Calendar spraying suppresses the pest and its natural enemies at the same time, but the enemies recover more slowly because their populations are smaller and their generation times longer. The result is a pesticide treadmill where each spray makes the next one more necessary. Threshold-based spraying breaks the loop, and the biodiversity gain shows up fastest of any intervention here because it is a removal of pressure rather than a slow build of structure.
interventions.trade_offs: Requires weekly scouting labour and the discipline to not spray when the field looks bad but is below threshold.

interventions.title: Gypsum plus organic amendment on sodic soil
interventions.what_to_do: Apply gypsum at the gypsum requirement dose with farmyard manure or pressmud, leach with good-quality water, and establish a salt-tolerant pioneer crop before the intended cash crop.
causal_chain: calcium displaces exchangeable sodium -> clay flocculates instead of dispersing
flocculation -> macropores reopen, infiltration and drainage recover
leaching removes sodium -> root zone becomes habitable
organic matter added -> microbial activity resumes, nutrient cycling restarts
vegetation cover returns -> further carbon input, positive feedback
interventions.why_it_works: Sodic soil fails physically, not just chemically: excess sodium disperses clay, the surface seals, and water cannot enter, so the soil is simultaneously waterlogged at the surface and droughted at depth. Gypsum alone reopens the structure but leaves the soil biologically dead; the organic amendment supplies the carbon that lets the microbial community recolonise. Applying only one of the two is the most common reason reclamation stalls.
interventions.trade_offs: Needs a drainage outlet and good-quality leaching water; without drainage the sodium simply redistributes. Gypsum cost is significant at the full requirement dose.

interventions.title: Vegetated riparian buffer along drains and streams
interventions.what_to_do: Leave or plant a 5-15 m multi-layer strip of native grasses, shrubs and trees along every watercourse and field drain; exclude cultivation, grazing and spraying from it.
causal_chain: dense root mat -> surface runoff slowed, sediment deposited before reaching water
root uptake plus denitrification in the saturated zone -> nitrate load falls
canopy shade -> stream temperature falls, dissolved oxygen rises
cooler oxygenated water -> aquatic invertebrate and fish diversity rise
continuous woody strip along a watercourse -> the most effective wildlife corridor in a farmed landscape
interventions.why_it_works: Riparian strips do double duty in a way few interventions manage: they are a water-quality filter and a movement corridor at the same time, because watercourses are already the natural connectivity skeleton of a landscape. The nitrate removal is largely microbial denitrification in the saturated root zone, which is why the strip has to reach the water table to work and why a mown grass verge underperforms a multi-layer strip.
interventions.trade_offs: Takes productive land nearest the water, which is often the most fertile. Effectiveness collapses where runoff is concentrated into a channel that cuts through the strip.

interventions.title: Biochar amendment co-applied with compost
interventions.what_to_do: Apply 2-10 t/ha of biochar produced from local crop residue, pre-charged by co-composting rather than applied fresh, banded into the root zone.
causal_chain: high-porosity carbon skeleton -> cation exchange capacity and water retention rise in sandy soil
pore network -> physical refuge for bacteria from protist predation
co-composting -> pores pre-loaded with nutrients and inoculum instead of stripping them from the soil
improved retention -> less nutrient leaching to groundwater
recalcitrant carbon -> long-residence-time carbon stock, distinct from labile organic matter
interventions.why_it_works: Biochar works on a different mechanism from ordinary organic matter: it is not food for microbes, it is housing. Its value is physical structure and exchange capacity, which is why the response is large on sandy low-CEC soils and often negligible on clays that already have both. Applying it fresh is the classic failure mode, because the empty pores adsorb nutrients out of the soil in the first season and yields dip.
interventions.trade_offs: Response on clay and already-alkaline soils is often nil or negative. Feedstock and pyrolysis quality vary enormously, and uncontrolled pyrolysis creates its own air pollution problem.

interventions.title: Alternate wetting and drying in irrigated rice
interventions.what_to_do: Install a perforated field water tube and re-irrigate only when the water table drops to about 15 cm below the surface, instead of maintaining continuous flooding.
causal_chain: soil periodically aerated -> methanogenic archaea suppressed -> methane emission falls
less pumping -> groundwater draw and energy use fall
aerobic phases -> root system deeper, lodging risk lower
reduced continuous flooding -> mosquito breeding and some pest cycles interrupted
caution: aeration can raise nitrous oxide, so the net climate effect depends on N management
interventions.why_it_works: Continuous flooding is an anaerobic engineering choice made for weed control, not because rice needs standing water. Removing the permanent anaerobic layer removes the habitat of the methane-producing archaea. The trade-off is real and worth stating: alternate aerobic and anaerobic phases can increase nitrous oxide, so the intervention only delivers a net greenhouse benefit when nitrogen is applied in split doses rather than broadcast.

effects.magnitude: can rise; depends on N management

interventions.trade_offs: Weed pressure rises without the flood. Needs reliable irrigation control, so it fails on rotational canal supply where the farmer cannot choose the timing.

interventions.title: Ground-nesting and cavity-nesting bee habitat provision
interventions.what_to_do: Keep small patches of bare, undisturbed, sun-exposed soil on well-drained ground away from tillage, and add stem bundles or drilled hardwood blocks on field edges.
causal_chain: undisturbed bare soil -> ground-nesting solitary bees can actually nest
nesting sites near forage -> local populations become resident, not transient
resident wild bees -> pollination service independent of rented hives
wild bee diversity -> pollination is more robust to weather because species differ in activity windows
diverse pollinator assemblage -> fruit set more reliable than with a single managed species
interventions.why_it_works: A majority of wild bee species nest in bare ground, and every biodiversity plan that adds flowers while leaving the whole farm tilled or mulched is offering food with no housing. Wild bee diversity also buys weather insurance: managed honeybees forage in a narrow temperature and wind window, while a diverse wild assemblage covers a much wider range of conditions, so fruit set holds up in a bad bloom week.
interventions.trade_offs: Counter-intuitive to farmers who treat bare soil as a failure. Artificial bee hotels need annual cleaning or they become disease and parasite traps.

interventions.title: Split and soil-test-based nitrogen application
interventions.what_to_do: Replace a single basal broadcast with 3-4 split doses timed to crop demand, dosed from a soil test or leaf colour chart rather than a fixed recommendation.
causal_chain: nitrogen supply matched to uptake curve -> less nitrate sitting in soil between rain events
less residual nitrate -> leaching to groundwater and runoff to surface water fall
lower nitrate load -> algal blooms and eutrophication downstream reduced
less ammonia volatilisation and nitrous oxide -> lower emissions per tonne of grain
reduced soil nitrogen surplus -> mycorrhizal association restored, which excess N suppresses
interventions.why_it_works: Nitrogen loss is a timing mismatch, not a dose problem. A single basal dose puts the whole season's nitrogen into the soil weeks before the crop can take it up, so the first heavy rain exports it. The biodiversity effect is mostly off-site and therefore easy to miss: the species that suffer from over-fertilisation are downstream aquatic ones, plus the mycorrhizal fungi that a high-nitrogen root zone makes redundant.
interventions.trade_offs: More field operations and more labour. Top-dressing needs a workable field, which heavy rain can prevent at exactly the moment the dose is due.

interventions.title: Multi-species shelterbelt on the windward boundary
interventions.what_to_do: Plant a 3-5 row shelterbelt of mixed native species with graded heights, aiming for roughly 50% porosity rather than a solid wall, perpendicular to the prevailing dry-season wind.
causal_chain: windspeed reduced for 10-20x the belt height downwind -> evapotranspiration demand falls
lower evaporative demand -> crop water stress and irrigation requirement fall
wind erosion of topsoil reduced -> nutrient-rich fine fraction retained
multi-species multi-height structure -> niches for birds, bats and insects a single-species row cannot offer
fruit and flower-bearing natives -> food resource across seasons, not just cover
interventions.why_it_works: A porous belt outperforms a solid one, which is the counter-intuitive part: a solid barrier creates turbulence and a short sheltered zone, while a 50% porous belt bleeds air through and extends the low-wind zone far downwind. Species mixture matters for the same reason it matters in a hedgerow, and a single-species exotic row delivers the wind benefit with almost none of the biodiversity benefit.
interventions.trade_offs: A shaded and root-competition strip immediately adjacent to the belt yields less; the net gain only appears when the sheltered zone is counted. 3-5 years to effect.

interventions.title: Restore hydrology and buffer zone of a degraded wetland
interventions.what_to_do: Remove or breach drainage structures to restore the natural hydroperiod, clear invasive water hyacinth mechanically, and establish an uncultivated buffer around the full seasonal high-water mark.
causal_chain: natural wetting and drying cycle restored -> native emergent plants outcompete invasives adapted to permanent water
emergent vegetation returns -> fish nursery and amphibian breeding habitat restored
buffer zone -> nutrient inflow that drives the invasion cut off at source
lower nutrient load -> algal dominance reduced, submerged plants and dissolved oxygen recover
functioning wetland -> flood attenuation and dry-season baseflow for the surrounding land
interventions.why_it_works: Most wetland degradation is a hydrology problem wearing a vegetation problem's clothes. Clearing water hyacinth without restoring the hydroperiod and cutting nutrient inflow buys a few months, because the altered, permanently flooded, nutrient-rich condition is exactly what the invasive is adapted to. Fixing the water regime changes which species wins by default, so the clearing only has to be done once.
interventions.trade_offs: Restoring the hydroperiod usually means someone loses drained land, so this is the most institutionally difficult intervention in the set. Mechanical invasive removal has to be repeated in year 1-2 before the native community closes.

interventions.title: Stabilise field bunds with deep-rooted native grasses
interventions.what_to_do: Plant vetiver or a local deep-rooted perennial grass along contour bunds and field boundaries; harvest the tops for fodder or thatch and never uproot the clumps.
causal_chain: dense vertical root curtain -> a living barrier that slows runoff without impounding it
sediment deposits upslope of the clump line -> terraces form naturally over several seasons
reduced runoff velocity -> infiltration and recharge rise
perennial tussocks -> overwintering and nesting habitat for grassland invertebrates and small birds
fodder offtake from the tops -> the practice pays for its own maintenance
interventions.why_it_works: The engineering value is the root curtain, not the shoot: vetiver roots go down several metres and form a near-continuous vertical screen that sediment cannot pass. Because it is a living structure it repairs itself after every storm, unlike an earthen bund that has to be rebuilt. It also provides the only perennial tussock habitat in an annually cultivated field, which matters for ground-nesting invertebrates.
interventions.trade_offs: Narrow strip of land taken along bunds. Choose a non-invasive local ecotype; some vigorous grasses become weeds in irrigated systems.

interventions.title: De-paving and native-species planting in peri-urban land
interventions.what_to_do: Break up unused impervious surface, replace ornamental exotics with locally native flowering and fruiting species, and connect the patches along existing drains and road verges.
causal_chain: impervious cover removed -> infiltration rises, storm runoff peak falls
native flowering species -> insect herbivores that exotic ornamentals cannot support return
native insects -> insectivorous birds and bats regain a food base
vegetated patches linked along verges -> isolated urban fragments become a connected network
canopy and soil moisture -> local surface temperature falls, urban heat island moderated
interventions.why_it_works: Ornamental urban planting fails ecologically because native insect herbivores are usually specialists that cannot eat exotic foliage, so an exotic-planted park is structurally green and trophically empty. Swapping species composition, not just adding more greenery, is what restores the food base. Connectivity does the rest, because urban habitat patches are small enough that isolated ones lose species steadily.

effects.magnitude: large gain versus exotic ornamental planting

interventions.trade_offs: Native species can look untidy against municipal expectations, so this usually needs a maintenance agreement before it needs a planting plan.

interventions.title: Arbuscular mycorrhizal inoculation with phosphorus restraint
interventions.what_to_do: Inoculate at sowing with a locally sourced AM fungal consortium and simultaneously cut phosphorus application to soil-test rates; avoid fungicide seed treatment in the same season.
causal_chain: hyphal network extends beyond the root depletion zone -> phosphorus and micronutrient uptake rise
glomalin and hyphal binding -> soil aggregate stability rises
stable aggregates -> physical protection of organic carbon from oxidation
networked root systems -> drought tolerance and seedling establishment improve
caveat: high available phosphorus switches the symbiosis off, so inoculating without cutting P wastes the input
interventions.why_it_works: The mycorrhizal symbiosis is a trade the plant only makes when phosphorus is scarce. Inoculating a soil that is already loaded with soluble phosphorus achieves nothing, which is why so many inoculation trials report no effect: the treatment was applied without removing the condition that suppresses it. The soil-structure benefit via glomalin is arguably larger than the nutrient benefit and is almost never measured.
interventions.trade_offs: Commercial inoculant quality is highly variable and often unverifiable. The effect is null in high-phosphorus soils, so this must be paired with the fertiliser change or not done at all.
